plan.topic_summary: Mixture of Experts (MoE) is a sparse model architecture that routes each input to a subset of specialized sub-networks, potentially reducing active compute per token relative to dense models of equivalent total capacity. The key question for a 1–5 year view is whether MoE can deliver sustained cost and quality advantages at scale, and what architectural or operational limits will constrain its dominance over dense alternatives.
key_questions: What is the current state of MoE adoption in production LLMs, and what inference cost savings are reported versus dense models at comparable quality?
What routing and load-balancing techniques are emerging to address expert underutilization and training instability, and how mature are they?
How does MoE scale in total parameter count and number of experts, and what are the observed diminishing returns or failure modes at larger scales?
What are the practical serving and memory constraints of MoE in production (e.g., expert offloading, inter-node communication), and how do they compare to dense model serving costs?
Will MoE become the default architecture for frontier-scale models over the next 3–5 years, or will hybrid or alternative sparse approaches (e.g., dynamic width, progressive activation) displace it?

gaps: Market evidence is very thin: only one small company (Maase Inc., CNY 33M revenue) appears in filings; no evidence on major players' MoE strategies or competitive positioning from company documents

No systematic evidence on MoE vs. dense model quality at comparable compute budgets at frontier scale; existing findings (R2, R9) flag that reported gains may be artifacts of routing collapse, but no positive large-scale comparison is cited
Frontier-scale training dynamics (100B+ parameters) are not directly evidenced in papers; R4 and R9 note that load-balancing remedies are only validated up to ~3B parameters, leaving a scale gap
Theoretical convergence result (S7) is unverified and rests on stylized models with limited Transformer-MoE validation
X findings provide context on the pace of MoE releases but are unverified social signals and cannot serve as factual evidence for the report

sources.title: Routing-Calibrated Expert Selection for MoE Reuse: Mechanism And Empirical Validation
sources.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
sources.abstract: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) efficiency research has followed three routes: improving the routing algorithm, pruning or compressing expert weights, and distilling expert knowledge into KV banks. All three share one property -- each introduces new content or a new selection criterion. This paper studies the opposite question: if an intermediate quantity has already been computed and is about to be discarded, can giving it a second consumer yield a capability gain? We call the mechanism reuse, and we give its criterion, its formalisation, measured effectiveness, and an analysis of why it works and when it fails. CRITERION. A quantity that has already been computed is used where it would not otherwise have been used. Operationally: it acquires a second consumer. In layer l, the routing distribution probs_l must be computed anyway; it serves only that layer's top-k selection and is then discarded, with no second consumer. FORMALISM. Because each token's top-k occupies exactly k mutually distinct slots, the per-layer hit rates r_e satisfy the exact identity sum_e r_e = k (measured: 4.0000, no approximation). Coverage and blood-loss are therefore exact quantities, and blood-loss is a linear functional of the resident set, so selecting the top-K experts by r_e is its exact minimiser. We name this rule RCES (Routing-Calibrated Expert Selection). We further define the coverage ceiling C_max(K) that no rule can exceed. TWO REUSE CHANNELS, BOTH WITH THE BACKBONE FROZEN. On Qwen1.5-MoE-A2.7B (24 layers / 60 experts / top-4), with every backbone parameter frozen: (a) phi channel. Pass probs_l through a 60x60 linear map phi_l and add it to the routing logits of layer l+1, changing which experts the next layer selects. Trainable parameters: 84,180 (0.00059% of the model). WikiText test perplexity falls from 9.485 to 9.094 (-4.13%). (b) SR channel (second routing), zero parameters, zero training. The first routing is the native top-4 and is left bit-for-bit untouched. The second routing appends, per token and per layer, the highest-ranked RCES experts that are not already active, weighted by their own native gate probability. Measured firing rate: 98.4% of tokens receive an append, averaging 1.84 of 2 slots, injecting 6.6% of the native routing weight. Cost: 0 new parameters, 0 training steps. MAIN RESULT (2044-question bank, paired McNemar). phi + SR improves task accuracy by +3.2 pp over the frozen backbone (61.8% vs 58.6%, p = 4.08e-4, 95% CI [+1.47, +4.99]) while holding the perplexity gain (-4.13%). On the non-numeric subset (1343 questions) the gain is also +3.2 pp (p = 7.17e-3). The SR channel alone -- zero parameters, zero training -- gives +1.8 pp (p = 8.88e-4). The two channels are additive: phi +1.4 pp, SR +1.8 pp, both +3.2 pp. A REFUTED EXPLANATION. A natural hypothesis is that reuse damages the native routing and the downstream layers can no longer read it. Against that: phi and phi+SR produce almost identical routing drift (0.2971 vs 0.2977; the native top-4 is unchanged for 36.0% vs 36.1% of token-layer pairs) while differing by 3.7 pp in task accuracy (p = 0.019). The SR channel structurally cannot alter the first routing, since it acts only on the dispatch output. What determines the task outcome is not how much the routing moved, but whether the information was put back. THE PLACEMENT LAW. These results, together with the earlier experiments in this line of work, condense into one statement in which the mechanism and the RCES criterion are held fixed and the only variable is where the mechanism is placed: any mechanism that intervenes in the FIRST routing -- that changes who is selected -- yields no task gain or active harm, while the same mechanism placed on the SECOND routing -- that appends one more computation -- yields a task gain. Hard masking (-38.3 pp), a large phi bias (-11.0 pp), and SR substitution all fall on the intervention side; SR appending (+1.8 pp) falls on the append side. The generative capability of the model is locked to the native routing distribution, and appending does not touch it. A MEASUREMENT WARNING. The 300-question bank reports the opposite sign for phi alone (-2.0 pp) and fails to resolve the phi+SR effect (+1.7 pp, p = 0.56). At 2044 questions all three comparisons become significant. Task-side claims in this area require the larger bank. A METHODOLOGICAL TRAP. "Zero weight is a no-op" is false on the evaluated hardware. The legacy expert dispatch padded the slot array with a zero-weight placeholder index, which left a duplicate token row inside an expert's input batch; the forward pass then diverged from the backbone (first divergence at layer 1, max routing-logit gap 1.0) and flipped 6 of 300 question verdicts, even though the platform itself reproduces bit-for-bit. Merging per-token weights and dropping zero-weight rows before the expert GEMM restores bit-identical output. ARTIFACTS. Source scripts, dependency modules, raw result files, the two phi checkpoints, and the exact cluster launch scripts are collected for reproduction.

sources.title: Not All Experts are Equal: Efficient Expert Pruning and Skipping for Mixture-of-Experts Large Language Models
sources.abstract: A pivotal advancement in the progress of large language models (LLMs) is the emergence of the Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) LLMs. Compared to traditional LLMs, MoE LLMs can achieve higher performance with fewer parameters, but it is still hard to deploy them due to their immense parameter sizes. Different from previous weight pruning methods that rely on specifically designed hardware, this paper mainly aims to enhance the deployment efficiency of MoE LLMs by introducing plug-and-play expert-level sparsification techniques. Specifically, we propose, for the first time to our best knowledge, post-training approaches for task-agnostic and task-specific expert pruning and skipping of MoE LLMs, tailored to improve deployment efficiency while maintaining model performance across a wide range of tasks. Extensive experiments show that our proposed methods can simultaneously reduce model sizes and increase the inference speed, while maintaining satisfactory performance. Data and code will be available at https://github.com/Lucky-Lance/Expert_Sparsity.

sources.title: ExpertFlow: Efficient Mixture-of-Experts Inference via Predictive Expert Caching and Token Scheduling
sources.abstract: Sparse Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models can outperform dense large language models at similar computation by activating only a small set of experts per token. However, stacking many expert modules introduces substantial parameter memory, which makes MoE models difficult to deploy in memory-constrained environments such as single-GPU devices. Offloading alleviates this issue by storing inactive experts in CPU memory and loading them on demand, but existing methods remain limited: static caches disregard input-dependent routing, and methods that train separate models to predict expert usage ahead of time are often inaccurate or require significant training cost. We propose ExpertFlow, a lightweight MoE inference system that addresses this routing dependency through three coordinated components: 1) a transformer-based routing path predictor that estimates expert usage across all MoE layers in a single forward pass, 2) a token scheduler that groups tokens with similar predicted routes to improve expert utilization, and 3) a predictive expert cache that loads only the required experts while correcting mispredictions at runtime. Together, these components enable efficient expert loading and execution, reducing GPU memory usage by up to 93.72% and improving inference throughput by up to 10x over strong offloading baselines on a single GPU.

sources.title: Stabilizing MoE Reinforcement Learning by Aligning Training and Inference Routers
sources.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) has emerged as a crucial approach for enhancing the capabilities of large language models. However, in Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models, the routing mechanism often introduces instability, even leading to catastrophic RL training collapse. We analyze the training-inference consistency of MoE models and identify a notable discrepancy in routing behaviors between the two phases. Moreover, even under identical conditions, the routing framework can yield divergent expert selections across repeated forward passes. To address this foundational inconsistency, we propose Rollout Routing Replay (R3), a method that records routing distributions from the inference engine and replays them during training. R3 significantly reduces training-inference policy KL divergence and mitigates extreme discrepancies without compromising training speed. Extensive experiments on various settings confirm that R3 succeeds in stabilizing RL training, preventing collapse and outperforming methods such as GSPO and TIS. We believe this work can offer a new solution for stabilizing RL in MoE models.

sources.title: Convergence Rates for Softmax Gating Mixture of Experts
sources.abstract: Mixture of experts (MoE) has recently emerged as an effective framework to advance the efficiency and scalability of machine learning models by softly dividing complex tasks among multiple specialized sub-models termed experts. Central to the success of MoE is an adaptive softmax gating mechanism which takes responsibility for determining the relevance of each expert to a given input and then dynamically assigning experts their respective weights. Despite its widespread use in practice, a comprehensive study on the effects of the softmax gating on the MoE has been lacking in the literature. To bridge this gap in this paper, we perform a convergence analysis of parameter estimation and expert estimation under the MoE equipped with the standard softmax gating or its variants, including a dense-to-sparse gating and a hierarchical softmax gating, respectively. Furthermore, our theories also provide useful insights into the design of sample-efficient expert structures. In particular, we demonstrate that it requires polynomially many data points to estimate experts satisfying our proposed \emph{strong identifiability} condition, namely a commonly used two-layer feed-forward network. In stark contrast, estimating linear experts, which violate the strong identifiability condition, necessitates exponentially many data points as a result of intrinsic parameter interactions expressed in the language of partial differential equations. All the theoretical results are substantiated with a rigorous guarantee.

sources.title: Rethinking MoE Routing for Commodity GPUs
sources.abstract: Commodity GPUs make large-model serving economically attractive, but they are typically connected via PCIe rather than high-bandwidth GPU fabrics. This is a poor fit for expert-parallel Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) inference, where each MoE layer routes tokens to selected experts via all-to-all communication, and PCIe crossings can become a major latency bottleneck. Existing serving systems and communication libraries optimize this traffic but treat router-selected expert assignments as fixed. We propose PCIe-MoE, an inference-time mechanism that decides when a low-confidence remote expert is worth a costly PCIe hop, and when a nearby, score-similar expert can be substituted instead. PCIe-MoE combines topology profiling, replaceability-aware placement, risk-aware remapping, and quality guards to reshape token-to-expert routing without retraining.

sources.title: Mixture-of-Experts Models in Vision: Routing, Optimization, and Generalization
sources.abstract: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architectures enable conditional computation by routing inputs to multiple expert subnetworks and are often motivated as a mechanism for scaling large language models. In this project, we instead study MoE behavior in an image classification setting, focusing on predictive performance, expert utilization, and generalization. We compare dense, SoftMoE, and SparseMoE classifier heads on the CIFAR10 dataset under comparable model capacity. Both MoE variants achieve slightly higher validation accuracy than the dense baseline while maintaining balanced expert utilization through regularization, avoiding expert collapse. To analyze generalization, we compute Hessian-based sharpness metrics at convergence, including the largest eigenvalue and trace of the loss Hessian, evaluated on both training and test data. We find that SoftMoE exhibits higher sharpness by these metrics, while Dense and SparseMoE lie in a similar curvature regime, despite all models achieving comparable generalization performance. Complementary loss surface perturbation analyses reveal qualitative differences in non-local behavior under finite parameter perturbations between dense and MoE models, which help contextualize curvature-based measurements without directly explaining validation accuracy. We further evaluate empirical inference efficiency and show that naively implemented conditional routing does not yield inference speedups on modern hardware at this scale, highlighting the gap between theoretical and realized efficiency in sparse MoE models.

sources.title: Statistic-Augmented, Decoupled MoE Routing and Aggregating in Autonomous Driving
sources.abstract: Autonomous driving (AD) scenarios are inherently complex and diverse, posing significant challenges for a single deep learning model to effectively cover all possible conditions, such as varying weather, traffic densities, and road types. Large Model (LM)-Driven Mixture of Experts (MoE) paradigm offers a promising solution, where LM serves as the backbone to extract latent features while MoE serves as the downstream head to dynamically select and aggregate specialized experts to adapt to different scenarios. However, routing and aggregating in MoE face intrinsic challenges, including imprecise expert selection due to flawed routing strategy and inefficient expert aggregation leading to suboptimal prediction. To address these issues, we propose a statistic-augmented, decoupled MoE }outing and Aggregating Mechanism (MoE-RAM) driven by LM. Specifically, on the one hand, MoE-RAM enhances expert routing by incorporating statistical retrieval mechanism to match LM-extracted latent features with cached prototypical features of the most relevant experts; on the other hand, MoE-RAM adaptively reweights experts' outputs in fusion by measuring statistical distances of experts' instant features against LM-extracted latent features. Benefiting from the synergy of the statistic-augmented MoE's routing and aggregating, MoE-RAM ultimately improves the prediction performance. We take the AD semantic segmentation task as an example to assess the proposed MoE-RAM. Extensive experiments on AD datasets demonstrate the superiority of MoE-RAM compared to other MoE baselines and conventional single-model approaches.

sources.title: Task-Conditioned Routing Signatures in Sparse Mixture-of-Experts Transformers
sources.abstract: Sparse Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architectures enable efficient scaling of large language models through conditional computation, yet the routing mechanisms responsible for expert selection remain poorly understood. In this work, we introduce routing signatures, a vector representation summarizing expert activation patterns across layers for a given prompt, and use them to study whether MoE routing exhibits task-conditioned structure. Using OLMoE-1B-7B-0125-Instruct as an empirical testbed, we show that prompts from the same task category induce highly similar routing signatures, while prompts from different categories exhibit substantially lower similarity. Within-category routing similarity (0.8435 +/- 0.0879) significantly exceeds across-category similarity (0.6225 +/- 0.1687), corresponding to Cohen's d = 1.44. A logistic regression classifier trained solely on routing signatures achieves 92.5% +/- 6.1% cross-validated accuracy on four-way task classification. To ensure statistical validity, we introduce permutation and load-balancing baselines and show that the observed separation is not explained by sparsity or balancing constraints alone. We further analyze layer-wise signal strength and low-dimensional projections of routing signatures, finding that task structure becomes increasingly apparent in deeper layers. These results suggest that routing in sparse transformers is not merely a balancing mechanism, but a measurable task-sensitive component of conditional computation. We release MOE-XRAY, a lightweight toolkit for routing telemetry and analysis.

sources.title: Guiding the Experts: Semantic Priors for Efficient and Focused MoE Routing
sources.abstract: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models have emerged as a promising direction for scaling vision architectures efficiently. Among them, Soft MoE improves training stability by assigning each token to all experts via continuous dispatch weights. However, current designs overlook the semantic structure which is implicitly encoded in these weights, resulting in suboptimal expert routing. In this paper, we discover that dispatch weights in Soft MoE inherently exhibit segmentation-like patterns but are not explicitly aligned with semantic regions. Motivated by this observation, we propose a foreground-guided enhancement strategy. Specifically, we introduce a spatially aware auxiliary loss that encourages expert activation to align with semantic foreground regions. To further reinforce this supervision, we integrate a lightweight LayerScale mechanism that improves information flow and stabilizes optimization in skip connections. Our method necessitates only minor architectural adjustments and can be seamlessly integrated into prevailing Soft MoE frameworks. Comprehensive experiments on ImageNet-1K and multiple smaller-scale classification benchmarks not only showcase consistent performance enhancements but also reveal more interpretable expert routing mechanisms.

sources.title: GEM: Graph-Enhanced Mixture-of-Experts with ReAct Agents for Dialogue State Tracking
sources.abstract: Dialogue State Tracking (DST) requires precise extraction of structured information from multi-domain conversations, a task where Large Language Models (LLMs) struggle despite their impressive general capabilities. We present GEM (Graph-Enhanced Mixture-of-Experts), a novel framework that combines language models and graph-structured dialogue understanding with ReAct agent-based reasoning for superior DST performance. Our approach dynamically routes between specialized experts: a Graph Neural Network that captures dialogue structure and turn-level dependencies, and a finetuned T5-Small encoder-decoder for sequence modeling, coordinated by an intelligent router. For complex value generation tasks, we integrate ReAct agents that perform structured reasoning over dialogue context. On MultiWOZ 2.2, GEM achieves 65.19% Joint Goal Accuracy, substantially outperforming end-to-end LLM approaches (best: 38.43%) and surpassing state-of-the-art (SOTA) methods including TOATOD (63.79%), D3ST (58.70%), and Diable (56.48%). Our graph-enhanced mixture-of-experts architecture with ReAct integration demonstrates that combining structured dialogue representation with dynamic expert routing and agent-based reasoning provides a powerful paradigm for dialogue state tracking, achieving superior accuracy while maintaining computational efficiency through selective expert activation.

sources.title: HERO-MoE: Historical Expert Routing with Scale-Preserving Fusion
sources.abstract: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architectures have become a standard way to scale model capacity while keeping computation sparse, yet routing remains a key determinant of MoE quality and training behavior. Prior empirical studies suggest that MoE routing reflects input semantics and upstream computation across depth, but standard routers do not explicitly use the routing distributions produced by preceding layers. We propose HERO-MoE, Historical Expert ROuting with Scale-Preserving Fusion, a routing framework that injects historical routing priors into MoE routers by reusing detached, dense routing distributions collected from preceding MoE layers. The key idea is simple: HERO-MoE preserves the original token-conditioned routing branch and adds a residual historical routing contribution before the standard softmax and top-$k$ dispatch. To stabilize this historical signal, HERO-MoE introduces a scale-preserving fusion mechanism that matches the magnitude of historical routing memory to the current hidden representation and accounts for the number of visible historical layers, without introducing an auxiliary routing loss or a fusion-specific tuning parameter. By reusing routing distributions already computed by preceding MoE layers, HERO-MoE improves training-loss reduction with modest end-to-end overhead. The resulting router remains compatible with standard sparse dispatch, including top-$k$ and group-limited routing, and can be inserted into existing MoE backbones with minimal architectural changes. Experiments on an approximately 8B-parameter MoE model with 0.5B active parameters, trained from scratch on 100B tokens, show that HERO-MoE reduces the final loss from 1.6393 to 1.6184, while peak memory and FLOPs increase by only 0.44\% and 0.64\%, respectively.

sources.title: Mixture of Experts with Soft Nearest Neighbor Loss: Resolving Expert Collapse via Representation Disentanglement
sources.abstract: The Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) model uses a set of expert networks that specialize on subsets of a dataset under the supervision of a gating network. A common issue in MoE architectures is ``expert collapse'' where overlapping class boundaries in the raw input feature space cause multiple experts to learn redundant representations, thus forcing the gating network into rigid routing to compensate. We propose an enhanced MoE architecture that utilizes a feature extractor network optimized using Soft Nearest Neighbor Loss (SNNL) prior to feeding input features to the gating and expert networks. By pre-conditioning the latent space to minimize distances among class-similar data points, we resolve structural expert collapse which results to experts learning highly orthogonal weights. We employ Expert Specialization Entropy and Pairwise Embedding Similarity to quantify this dynamic. We evaluate our experimental approach across four benchmark image classification datasets (MNIST, FashionMNIST, CIFAR10, and CIFAR100), and we show our SNNL-augmented MoE models demonstrate structurally diverse experts which allow the gating network to adopt a more flexible routing strategy. This paradigm significantly improves classification accuracy on the FashionMNIST, CIFAR10, and CIFAR100 datasets.

sources.title: Lifecycle Mixture of Experts: Staggered Death Prevents Expert Collapse in Mutual Activation MoE
sources.abstract: Abstract re of Experts (MoE) architectures su er from expert collapse, where experts converge to homogeneous representations during training, nullifying the bene ts of conditional computation. We study the mutual activation MoE a router-free architecture where experts activate each other through sigmoid-gated cross-connections and show that collapse is inevitable under standard training (mean pairwise cosine similarity > 0.93). We propose Lifecycle MoE, a mechanism that detects collapse via similarity and cross-activation metrics, then kills and rebirths experts to restore di erentiation. Our key nding is that staggered death killing only one expert at a time with a cooldown period preserves system stability while breaking collapse, achieving T2 accuracy within 0.5pp of baseline (vs. 48pp degradation with simultaneous death). Extended 120-epoch training reveals a self-stabilization property: only a single death event is needed to permanently prevent re-collapse, with consensus accuracy reaching 62.57% (vs. 49.19% baseline, a +13.4pp gain). We further show that snapshot-based revival and similarity-targeted death are redundant or counterproductive, while Linear-capacity experts naturally resist collapse. These results establish staggered lifecycle as a simple, e ective, and self-limiting mechanism for maintaining expert diversity in mutual activation MoE.

sources.title: SimSMoE: Toward Efficient Training Mixture of Experts via Solving Representational Collapse
sources.venue: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: NAACL
sources.abstract: Sparse mixture of experts (SMoE) have emerged as an effective approach for scaling large language models while keeping a constant computational cost.Regardless of several notable successes of SMoE, effective training such architecture remains elusive due to the representation collapse problem, which in turn harms model performance and causes parameter redundancy.In this work, we present Similarity-based Sparse Mixture of Experts (SimSMoE), a novel similarity of neural network algorithm, that guarantees a solution to address the representation collapse issue between experts given a fixed FLOPs budget.We conduct extensive empirical evaluations on three large language models for both Pre-training and Fine-tuning tasks to illustrate the efficacy, robustness, and scalability of our method.The results demonstrate that SimSMoE significantly enhances existing routing policy and outperforms other SMoE routing methods in performance for the tasks.Our implementation is publicly available at https://github.com/ giangdip2410/SimSMoE.

sources.title: Softmax Routing Dynamics in Mixture-of-Experts Models: Collapse and Recovery
sources.abstract: Softmax routing in mixture-of-experts models can concentrate probability on a subset of experts, suppressing access to the others. We study how this concentration forms, why it persists, and how suppressed probabilities recover. For fixed experts, a stationary-loss barrier identifies the face supporting the optimal routed output. In a common-target square-loss model with freely trainable expert outputs, slow adaptation tracks fixed-expert dynamics on finite horizons, while every fixed positive adaptation rate yields an interior routing limit. An exact normal-velocity decomposition separates complementary-expert covariance from relative gradient advantage. Under positive two-sided power bounds along recovery paths, uniform over initial masses, the resulting coefficient's order of vanishing gives logarithmic or power-law recovery times. Integrations of constructed fields reproduce these orders. An exact discrete log-odds identity relates neural updates to threshold crossing. In paired Transformer-MoE training, removing a class-conditional router-gradient contrast delays confirmed recovery and reduces accumulated log-odds on fixed tokens, both with and without capacity constraints.

sources.title: Routing Collapse in Classification-Head-Based Mixture-of-Experts Models for Aspect-Based Sentiment Analysis
sources.venue: IEEE International Conference on Information Reuse and Integration (IRI)
sources.abstract: Aspect-Based Sentiment Analysis (ABSA) requires identifying opinion targets and predicting the sentiment directed at each-a granularity that aggregate ratings cannot provide. We investigate whether a classification-head Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architecture, knowledge distillation, and gradient-based token attribution can jointly improve accuracy, efficiency, and transparency on this task. Our central finding is that the MoE's performance gain over a single-head BERT baseline stems not from expert specialization but from routing collapse: one expert dominates all predictions with a routing weight of$\approx 1.0$, making the model functionally equivalent to a deeper single MLP. This collapse also limits the benefit of subsequent knowledge distillation. These results underscore the importance of routing diagnostics and capacity-matched baselines when evaluating MoE systems in low-resource classification settings.

sources.title: De-collapsing User Intent: Adaptive Diffusion Augmentation with Mixture-of-Experts for Sequential Recommendation
sources.venue: Proceedings of the AAAI Conference on Artificial Intelligence
sources.abstract: Sequential recommendation (SR) aims to predict users' next action based on their historical behavior, and is widely adopted by a number of platforms. The performance of SR models relies on rich interaction data. However, in real-world scenarios, many users only have a few historical interactions, leading to the problem of data sparsity. Data sparsity not only leads to model overfitting on sparse sequences, but also hinders the model’s ability to capture the underlying hierarchy of user intents. This results in misinterpreting the user's true intents and recommending irrelevant items. Existing data augmentation methods attempt to mitigate overfitting by generating relevant and varied data. However, they overlook the problem of reconstructing the user's intent hierarchy, which is lost in sparse data. Consequently, the augmented data often fails to align with the user's true intents, potentially leading to misguided recommendations. To address this, we propose the Adaptive Diffusion Augmentation for Recommendation (ADARec) framework. Critically, instead of using a diffusion model as a black-box generator, we use its entire step-wise denoising trajectory to reconstruct a user's intent hierarchy from a single sparse sequence. To ensure both efficiency and effectiveness, our framework adaptively determines the required augmentation depth for each sequence and employs a specialized mixture-of-experts architecture to decouple coarse- and fine-grained intents. Experiments show ADARec outperforms state-of-the-art methods on standard benchmarks and on sparse sequences, demonstrating its ability to reconstruct hierarchical intent representations from sparse data.

sources.title: Localising Context Length Degradation in a Mixture of Experts Language Model: Retrieval Head Collapse, Not Router Failure
sources.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
sources.abstract: Long-context "context rot" (accuracy degradation as input length grows, even when task difficulty is held fixed) is localized here to a specific, causal mechanism inside a small Mixture-of-Experts language model (OLMoE-1B-7B-0924), then tested for generality across two further architectures. Forced-choice retrieval accuracy falls from 0.938 (256 tokens) to 0.688 (3,840 tokens) on a controlled needle-in-a-haystack substrate. A deconfounded linear probe shows the target fact remains ~99.5% decodable at its source position on every failing prompt, ruling out storage loss; decodability specifically at the readout position degrades instead (0.714 vs. 0.960 on model-right prompts). Sixteen attention heads, identified from short prompts alone, carry that content to the readout; on long failing prompts their attention to the fact collapses (0.432 to 0.187), localized to those heads well beyond a random-head null (specificity p<0.0005). A pre-softmax attention boost restricted to exactly those 16 heads, over the fact's span, repairs all 14 failing prompts against strength-matched random-head and wrong-span controls (answer probability 0.238 to 0.986, dz=5.55). Three router-level and readout-level interventions were tried first and failed: two that verifiably restored MoE specialist routing did not move accuracy, and a residual-stream content injection at the readout was content-independent — showing router "starvation" is a downstream correlate of the transport failure, not its cause. The full causal chain of head identification, localized collapse, and causal repair replicates on a second, architecturally distinct MoE (Granite-3.0-3B-A800M: 5/5 failures repaired against matched controls) and on a dense transformer with no MoE component at all (Pythia-2.8B: 11/11 repaired, dz=1.33-1.44; the collapse measurement itself on this substrate is significant and specific but falls under the project's own effect-size floor, and is reported as suggestive rather than confirmatory). This indicates the attention-transport failure and its repair do not depend on Mixture-of-Experts routing. A training-free, IDF-weighted lexical detector, requiring zero forward passes of the model under study, locates the failing span and recovers 100.8% and 99.4% of the oracle repair on the two primary OLMoE substrates, 99.1% on Granite, and 51% on a harder Pythia substrate built specifically to weaken lexical anchoring. Its boundary was tested, not assumed. It is unaffected by paraphrase (100% hit, 100.8% of oracle) but fails completely on multi-hop composition as a single pass (0% hit); a training-free two-stage chain recovers 45.0% of the oracle effect there with no labels, and a registered labeled fallback recovers 61.4%. A follow-up track replaces lexical overlap with sentence embeddings and a graph walk specifically to test coreference, where the relevant content shares zero tokens with the question by construction. The result is a registered split, not a single verdict: a discourse-adjacency edge fully solves coreference where the referring expression is immediately adjacent to its antecedent (100% of oracle, 22 of 22 repaired), but on a harder substrate with antecedent distance drawn independently per prompt, both that mechanism and a distance-tolerant version built specifically to extend it fail identically past distance one (dz=0.48). Both are reported as registered negative results, not discarded. Every claim above is preregistered before evaluation, with effect-size floors (|d| or |dz| >= 0.8) alongside significance, sign-flip and label-shuffle permutation tests (2,000 draws), matched controls, and Benjamini-Hochberg FDR correction. Results that miss a registered bar are reported as such rather than dropped — including three failed intervention families, an initially wrong lexical-detector prediction (logged and corrected), and both coreference negative results above.

sources.title: Sparse Mixture-of-Experts Routing in Visual Diffusion Transformers:Diagnosis, Boundary Calibration and Evolutionary Roadmap from Routing Collapse to Selective Deadlock
sources.abstract: This paper systematically diagnoses the training failure modes of Token-Choice sparse Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) on video Diffusion Transformers. Starting from a pretrained dense model of about 5 billion parameters, we convert it into an MoE architecture following three laws: routed experts exactly clone the original FFN weights, shared experts are initialized to zero for verification and then to extremely small non-zero noise for actual training, while only the gating networks start from random initialization. Experiments reveal a hierarchy of five failure modes: (1) linear routers suffer global soft saturation with complete expert homogenization; (2) MLP routers introduce selective deadlock, where roughly one-third of layers degenerate into a single-expert mode that cannot be prevented by increasing the auxiliary loss; (3) cross-attention routers exhibit preliminary self-recovery, yet about nine layers remain stubbornly deadlocked; (4) deadlocked layers display a U-shaped distribution, concentrated in shallow visual processing layers and deep semantic integration layers; (5) bfloat16 mixed precision causes tiny weight updates to be truncated to zero by hardware. Based on routing decision time series over 65 million tokens across 5,000 training steps, we propose the Functional Redundancy Hypothesis: deadlock is a rational waiting strategy before the shared expert matures within the gate-shared expert-routed expert triadic system. This hypothesis is supported by the theory of functional redundancy in systems biology. On the engineering side, we summarize the Three Laws of dense-to-MoE conversion and provide a complete solution for the bfloat16 precision trap. We calibrate the current capability boundary of the Token-Choice paradigm and outline a three-step evolutionary roadmap from visual unification to a world model.

sources.title: Auxiliary-Loss-Free Load Balancing Strategy for Mixture-of-Experts
sources.abstract: For Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models, an unbalanced expert load will lead to routing collapse or increased computational overhead. Existing methods commonly employ an auxiliary loss to encourage load balance, but a large auxiliary loss will introduce non-negligible interference gradients into training and thus impair the model performance. In order to control load balance while not producing undesired gradients during training, we propose Loss-Free Balancing, featured by an auxiliary-loss-free load balancing strategy. To be specific, before the top-K routing decision, Loss-Free Balancing will first apply an expert-wise bias to the routing scores of each expert. By dynamically updating the bias of each expert according to its recent load, Loss-Free Balancing can consistently maintain a balanced distribution of expert load. In addition, since Loss-Free Balancing does not produce any interference gradients, it also elevates the upper bound of model performance gained from MoE training. We validate the performance of Loss-Free Balancing on MoE models with up to 3B parameters trained on up to 200B tokens. Experimental results show that Loss-Free Balancing achieves both better performance and better load balance compared with traditional auxiliary-loss-controlled load balancing strategies.

sources.title: DeepSeekMoE: Towards Ultimate Expert Specialization in Mixture-of-Experts Language Models
sources.venue: Proceedings of the conference - Association for Computational Linguistics. Meeting
sources.abstract: Damai Dai, Chengqi Deng, Chenggang Zhao, R.x. Xu, Huazuo Gao, Deli Chen, Jiashi Li, Wangding Zeng, Xingkai Yu, Y. Wu, Zhenda Xie, Y.k. Li, Panpan Huang, Fuli Luo, Chong Ruan, Zhifang Sui, Wenfeng Liang. Proceedings of the 62nd Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics (Volume 1: Long Papers). 2024.

sources.title: MoE-LLaVA: Mixture of Experts for Large Vision-Language Models
sources.abstract: Recently, remarkable progress has been made in scaling up Large Language Models (LLMs) through the use of the sparse Mixture-of-Expert (MoE) layers without significantly increasing computational cost. However, the transition from a pre-trained LLM to a sparse Large Vision-Language Model (LVLM) with MoE remains an open challenge. Directly fine-tuning an LLM to a sparse LVLM often leads to training collapse, characterized by (1) a large modality feature distribution gap and (2) expert load imbalance. This paper proposes a three-stage decoupled weight training process. In the first two stages, the model learns to adapt the LLM to an LVLM. In the third stage, the FFN weights from the second stage are used as lossless initialization for expert weights, effectively constructing a sparse model with a vast number of parameters while maintaining constant computational cost. Through extensive ablation experiments, we derive three empirical guidelines and propose a sparse LVLM termedMoE-LLaVA. MoE-LLaVA is a MoE-based sparse LVLM architecture, which uniquely activates only the top-$k$experts through routers during deployment, keeping the remaining experts inactive. Extensive experiments demonstrate that MoE-LLaVA outperforms LLaVA-1.5-7B with an average improvement of 4.6 across nine visual understanding benchmarks. Notably, with only 2.2B active parameters, our MoE-LLaVA shows comparable result with LLaVA-1.5-13B (87.0 vs. 85.9) on POPE benchmark. Our work establishes a baseline for sparse LVLMs and provides empirical guidelines for exploring the sparse LVLMs. Our code is available at:https://github.com/PKU-YuanGroup/MoE-LLaVA.

sources.title: Efficient MoE Serving in the Memory-Bound Regime: Balance Activated Experts, Not Tokens
sources.abstract: Expert Parallelism (EP) permits Mixture of Experts (MoE) models to scale beyond a single GPU. To address load imbalance across GPUs in EP, existing approaches aim to balance the number of tokens each GPU processes. Surprisingly, we find that this objective degrades performance rather than improving it when processing is memory-bound - a common occurrence in MoE serving, especially in the decode phase. Our analysis reveals that balancing the number of tokens processed per GPU increases the number of activated experts, exacerbating memory pressure in the memory-bound regime. We propose Minimum Expert Token ROuting, a novel token-routing algorithm for high-performance expert-parallel MoE serving in the memory-bound regime that balances the number of activated experts per GPU rather than token counts. METRO achieves near-optimal routing quality with minimal computational overhead by jointly optimizing algorithmic efficiency and leveraging the GPU's parallel processing power. To guarantee routing quality, METRO also employs a novel allGather scheme to gather global top-k knowledge, which has minimal overhead compared to conventional allToAll. Our evaluation of METRO against EPLB on both real systems (vLLM over 8 A100 GPUs) and a proprietary simulator (8-16 B200 GPUs) shows that METRO reduces decode latency by 11 - 22%, and total token throughput by 3 - 21% for Qwen3 and DeepSeek-V3 serving, where prefill and decode phases are co-deployed. In addition, by trading latency headroom for throughput, METRO improves decode throughput by up to 4.11x over EPLB at a fixed decode SLO.

findings.claim: Expert or routing collapse recurs across independent MoE settings (classification, LLM pre-training, diffusion transformers, sparse vision-language models). It looks like a structural training risk, not an isolated bug, and the conditional-computation benefit may not materialize in practice.
findings.label: verified_fact
findings.rationale: Six of the twelve papers frame collapse (representation, expert, routing or training collapse) as the central problem. Several are arXiv or Research Square preprints and are not peer reviewed. The settings differ widely, which supports generality, but the evidence is abstract-level only.
findings.supporting_excerpt: effective training such architecture remains elusive due to the representation collapse problem, which in turn harms model performance and causes parameter redundancy.

findings.claim: Reported MoE accuracy gains can be an artifact. In one ABSA study the gain over a single-head baseline came from one expert dominating (routing collapse), not from specialization, so the model behaved like a deeper single MLP. Without routing diagnostics and capacity-matched baselines, MoE benefits can be misattributed.
findings.label: verified_fact
findings.rationale: This is a single abstract on a small, low-resource classification task. It may not carry over to large LLM MoEs, but it shows the evaluation-methodology risk.
findings.supporting_excerpt: the MoE's performance gain over a single-head BERT baseline stems not from expert specialization but from routing collapse

findings.claim: Converting dense models to sparse MoE can fail in ways that standard mitigations do not fix. In a ~5B video diffusion transformer, MLP routers left about one-third of layers in single-expert deadlock, and increasing the auxiliary loss did not prevent it. bfloat16 truncation of small updates was also reported as a failure mode.
findings.label: verified_fact
findings.rationale: This is a single arXiv preprint with a specific upcycling recipe, so the failure modes may be setup-dependent. The 'Functional Redundancy Hypothesis' is the authors' own interpretation and is not independently tested here. The abstract is truncated.
findings.supporting_excerpt: MLP routers introduce selective deadlock, where roughly one-third of layers degenerate into a single-expert mode that cannot be prevented by increasing the auxiliary loss

findings.claim: Load balancing involves a trade-off. Auxiliary balancing losses can interfere with training and hurt quality, while alternatives are only demonstrated at modest scale (up to 3B parameters, 200B tokens). Their behavior at frontier scale is not shown in the abstract.
findings.label: ai_interpretation
findings.rationale: The first paper states that large auxiliary losses introduce interfering gradients. It validates its fix only up to 3B parameters and 200B tokens. It is an arXiv preprint, though widely cited (279). The diffusion-transformer preprint separately reports that a larger auxiliary loss did not prevent deadlock. The scale gap is my inference, not a result in either paper.

findings.claim: MoE inference efficiency is hardware- and regime-dependent. Standard token-balancing for expert parallelism can degrade performance when serving is memory-bound, so the 'constant compute' framing does not translate into simple serving gains.
findings.label: verified_fact
findings.rationale: This is an arXiv preprint. Part of the evaluation uses a proprietary simulator (8-16 B200 GPUs), which limits reproducibility. Real-system tests are on 8 A100 GPUs only. The reported improvements (11-22% decode latency) are moderate. The paper is a proposed fix, so it also shows that existing production balancing approaches (EPLB) are suboptimal in this regime.
findings.supporting_excerpt: balancing the number of tokens processed per GPU increases the number of activated experts, exacerbating memory pressure in the memory-bound regime.

findings.claim: Adapting pretrained dense models into sparse MoE is fragile. Direct fine-tuning of an LLM into a sparse vision-language MoE often causes training collapse, and a multi-stage recipe is required. This adds engineering complexity and process dependence.
findings.label: verified_fact
findings.rationale: The MoE-LLaVA abstract describes the collapse and its three-stage workaround, and the diffusion preprint reports similar conversion difficulties. The abstract also stresses constant computational cost with 'a vast number of parameters', but says nothing about memory footprint. That is a gap, not a demonstrated failure.
findings.supporting_excerpt: Directly fine-tuning an LLM to a sparse LVLM often leads to training collapse

findings.claim: Router-level fixes may not address some MoE failures. In OLMoE-1B-7B, long-context degradation was traced to collapse of specific attention heads. Interventions that restored MoE routing did not improve accuracy, so router symptoms there were correlates, not causes.
findings.label: ai_interpretation
findings.rationale: This is a Zenodo preprint, not peer reviewed, on a single small model with a controlled needle-in-a-haystack task. The abstract mentions only 14 failing prompts for the repair test, so generality to production-scale MoEs is unknown. It also cuts against a simple 'better routing fixes quality' narrative.
findings.supporting_excerpt: Forced-choice retrieval accuracy falls from 0.938 (256 tokens) to 0.688 (3,840 tokens) on a controlled needle-in-a-haystack substrate.

findings.claim: Softmax routing theory suggests collapse can persist, and recovery may be slow (logarithmic or power-law). However, the formal results rest on stylized models, such as a common-target square-loss setup, with only limited paired Transformer-MoE validation.
findings.label: ai_interpretation
findings.rationale: This is an arXiv preprint (2026-10) with no citations yet. The abstract states that concentration persists and that recovery times follow logarithmic or power-law orders under assumed bounds. The mapping from theory to large practical MoEs is not shown in the abstract.
findings.supporting_excerpt: Softmax routing in mixture-of-experts models can concentrate probability on a subset of experts, suppressing access to the others.

findings.claim: Proposed collapse remedies rest on narrow or non-standard evidence: small image-classification benchmarks, or a router-free 'mutual activation' architecture with modest absolute accuracy (62.57%). Their relevance to large-scale language MoEs is unestablished.
findings.label: ai_interpretation
findings.rationale: Both are preprints (arXiv, Research Square) with zero citations. The SNNL paper reports accuracy gains on three of four datasets (FashionMNIST, CIFAR10, CIFAR100), not on MNIST. The Lifecycle MoE paper reports that collapse was 'inevitable' under its own standard training. Both use settings far from production LLM MoEs.

hype_flags: 'Guarantees a solution' to representation collapse (SimSMoE): an absolute framing, supported in the abstract only by empirical evaluation.
'Towards Ultimate Expert Specialization' (DeepSeekMoE title): a strong framing that cannot be checked here because the supplied abstract has no technical content.
'Constant computational cost' for sparse MoE: this framing ignores memory-bound serving regimes and the memory needed to hold all experts, as the serving paper's results suggest.
'Resolving'/'preventing' expert collapse (SNNL, Lifecycle MoE): demonstrated only on small benchmarks or non-standard architectures, with no large-scale evidence.
MoE accuracy gains presented as evidence of specialization: one ABSA study found a gain explained by a single dominant expert.

finding.claim: S1 says routing, not expert architecture, is the 'dominant problem' across MoE papers. That conclusion comes from a retrieval sample that was probably routing-focused, and it is not a measured share of the field. The same evidence set includes expert pruning (S2), offloading and caching (S3), serving-side token balancing (R5) and theory (S7), none of which is routing-quality work. Several of the six cited papers are zero- or low-citation 2025-2026 preprints or Zenodo uploads. Other evidence (src_fd0ecc44fe) shows router-level symptoms can be downstream correlates and not the root cause.
finding.label: ai_interpretation
finding.rationale: This is a sampling and generalization problem. The finding counts the papers it retrieved. It treats that count as a statement about where MoE research effort or the bottleneck lies. The abstracts show MoE work addressing memory, serving and pruning as well. At least one paper finds that repairing routing did not repair the failure.

finding.claim: S6 says two papers reuse prior-layer routing distributions 'without retraining the backbone'. Only HERO-MoE describes prior-layer reuse. Its abstract reports 'improves training-loss reduction', which implies the router is trained, so 'without retraining' does not clearly apply. The Zenodo paper (src_b9f61d861b) frames reuse as selecting resident top-K experts by hit rate, with a frozen backbone. The abstract is cut off and does not show it improves routing quality using earlier layers' distributions. The two papers are also not shown to be the same technique, and both are unreviewed 2026 preprints with ~0-1 citations.
finding.label: ai_interpretation
finding.rationale: The synthesis merges two different mechanisms into one 'recurring direction'. The retraining claim holds, at most, for one paper. Calling them 'independent' corroboration overstates what two non-peer-reviewed preprints can show.
finding.supporting_excerpt: HERO-MoE improves training-loss reduction with modest end-to-end overhead.
finding.guard_note: relabelled ai_interpretation: a challenge is a judgement; its quoted excerpt was checked against the source

finding.claim: S3 is labelled verified_fact, but the 93.72% memory reduction and 10x throughput are author-reported best-case ('up to') figures from a single preprint. They are measured against offloading baselines on a single GPU, not against a model that fits in memory. The abstract also does not report accuracy effects, so no quality cost is ruled out. Other evidence (R5) shows MoE serving gains depend on hardware and regime, so these numbers should not be read as general.
finding.label: ai_interpretation
finding.rationale: The abstract confirms the paper makes this claim. It does not verify that the result holds. 'Up to' maxima against selected baselines in a single setting are weak evidence, and 'verified_fact' overstates their status.
finding.supporting_excerpt: reducing GPU memory usage by up to 93.72% and improving inference throughput by up to 10x over strong offloading baselines on a single GPU.
finding.guard_note: relabelled ai_interpretation: a challenge is a judgement; its quoted excerpt was checked against the source

finding.claim: S8 is labelled verified_fact, but the PCIe-MoE abstract contains no quantitative results. It describes a proposed mechanism with 'quality guards' and says nothing about how much accuracy substituting experts costs or how much latency it saves. The finding states as established that routing 'can be reshaped' at inference time to fit commodity hardware. The evidence supports only that the paper proposes this. The paper is a 0-citation workshop paper.
finding.label: ai_interpretation
finding.rationale: Replacing router-chosen experts with 'score-similar' ones can degrade quality, and the abstract gives no measurement of that. A proposal should be labelled as one, not as a verified fact, until results are visible.

finding.claim: S5 generalizes from one small model. The routing-signature result comes from OLMoE-1B-7B-Instruct, on four task categories, using a classifier on routing signatures. This shows routing correlates with task type. It does not show routing is functionally task-conditioned or that the pattern holds for other MoE models. Separate evidence (src_fd0ecc44fe) indicates routing patterns can be downstream correlates and not causal drivers, which cautions against reading structure as function.
finding.label: ai_interpretation
finding.rationale: Correlational findings from a single arXiv preprint and a single model are being used as 'empirical evidence' of a general property.

finding.claim: S10 describes GEM (dialogue state tracking) as an example of MoE routing used as a 'downstream modular head' alongside backbones. The abstract describes a router choosing between two heterogeneous components, a GNN and a T5-Small, plus ReAct agents. That is not a sparse MoE layer in the sense of the LLM-scale MoE work in the other findings. Grouping it with them makes the 'diverse domain adoption' trend look stronger than it is. Both cited papers are single, uncited preprints with author-reported results.
finding.label: ai_interpretation
finding.rationale: The word 'MoE' is shared, but the architecture differs. Two cases do not establish a trend.
finding.supporting_excerpt: dynamically routes between specialized experts: a Graph Neural Network that captures dialogue structure and turn-level dependencies, and a finetuned T5-Small encoder-decoder

finding.claim: S9 generalizes to 'vision settings' from a single CIFAR10 classifier-head study. The study compares only dense, SoftMoE and SparseMoE heads at small scale. The finding's own caveat, 'scale- and implementation-dependent', is not backed by tests across scales in this abstract. It shows only a naive implementation at one small scale, not a pattern across vision MoE.
finding.label: ai_interpretation
finding.rationale: The quoted wording is limited to 'at this scale'. The finding's wider framing, 'in vision settings', goes beyond it.
finding.supporting_excerpt: naively implemented conditional routing does not yield inference speedups on modern hardware at this scale
finding.guard_note: relabelled ai_interpretation: a challenge is a judgement; its quoted excerpt was checked against the source

finding.claim: S7 carries the label 'unverified_claim', but its content is stated in the cited abstract: polynomially many samples for two-layer feed-forward experts under strong identifiability, exponentially many for linear experts. The label is inconsistent. More important, the result is a theoretical statement about a specific parametric model with softmax gating. The finding gives no caveat that this may not transfer to practical LLM-scale sparse MoE.
finding.label: unverified_claim
finding.rationale: The label understates what the abstract supports. The finding also omits the idealized-model scope of the theory, and the abstract shown is cut off before its empirical substantiation.
finding.supporting_excerpt: it requires polynomially many data points to estimate experts satisfying our proposed strong identifiability condition, namely a commonly used two-layer feed-forward network.
finding.guard_note: downgraded from verified_fact: supporting excerpt missing or not found in the cited source text

limitations: Analysis is based on abstracts only (text_depth abstract_only); no methods, ablations or full results were read.
Only 12 papers, many arXiv/Research Square/Zenodo preprints that are not peer reviewed and have zero citations.
DeepSeekMoE's abstract is only an author list, and ADARec's (src_0a8ba5aefa) is truncated and about recommendation, so neither supports concrete risk claims.

The search skews toward 'collapse'. It gives little evidence on other risks such as security, inference memory footprint, communication overhead, cost, or competing architectures (dense models, state-space models). Their absence is a coverage gap, not evidence they are not risks.
Several sources are small-scale or non-LLM (MNIST/CIFAR, ABSA, a 1B-7B model), so extrapolation to frontier-scale MoEs is uncertain.
Dates and venue labels (e.g. MoE-LLaVA listed as 2026 in a journal) are taken as given from metadata.

Only titles, abstracts and metadata were available, and several abstracts are cut off. Challenges based on what an abstract omits (for example missing quality metrics) may be resolved in the full papers, which I did not read.
I could not independently verify any author-reported numbers.
Many cited papers are 2026 preprints or Zenodo uploads with 0-1 citations. I treated them as weakly corroborated, but this is a judgement and not a verified assessment of their quality.
The challenges rest on a small evidence set of 24 papers, so absence of contrary evidence here is not evidence of absence in the wider literature.
S2, S4 and S11 were left unchallenged because their abstracts support the findings as stated.

sources.title: DATA-AWARE MIXTURE OF EXPERTS AGENTIC QUERY [US20260359291A1]
sources.abstract: Techniques for generating and verifying Structured Query Language (SQL) queries are disclosed. In some embodiments, a system, a process, and/or a computer program product for generating and verifying SQL queries includes receiving a query that includes a user prompt associated with a user and directing the query to one of a plurality of expert modules based on content in the query using a router agent, wherein each expert module of the plurality of expert modules includes a plurality of agents; converting the user prompt into one or more optimized prompts using a prompt optimization agent; generating an SQL query based on the one or more optimized prompts and contextual information about a database using an SQL generation agent; and executing the generated SQL query against the database to generate query results and verifying whether the query results satisfy predetermined criteria using an execution and verification agent.

sources.title: Reinforcement learning based expert routing for mixture of experts language models [US12792925B1]
sources.abstract: Embodiments disclosed herein may use reinforcement learning techniques to train a gating network and optimize routing policy. Reinforcement learning may allow for an immediate reward (or penalty as the case may be) such that the desired actions can be rewarded and undesired actions can be penalized. The routing policy optimized using reinforcement learning may move away from the inflexible approach of the conventional gating networks and offer a desired level of flexibility for any type of query. Additionally, the gating network may be continuously trained upon deployment.

sources.title: DYNAMIC PARALLELISM FOR LANGUAGE MODEL INFERENCE [US20260350380A1]
sources.abstract: [0000]    Various examples relate to dynamic parallelism for language model inference. A pool of processing units is reconfigured between different parallelism modes during inference. In a first mode for attention computation, contextual memory data is distributed across processing units. After attention computation, the units are reprovisioned into a second mode with multi-dimensional parallelism, having tensor parallelism and sparse computation dimensions. The second mode enables processing tokens through neural networks in a sparse computation architecture. For dense models without mixture-of-experts, the sparse computation dimension equals one, allowing graceful degradation to tensor-parallel execution. Collective communication operations may facilitate transitions between modes while maintaining mathematical equivalence with non-distributed computation.

sources.abstract: [0000]    One aspect of the present disclosure relates to a question-and-answer system used in manufacturing sites, and more particularly, to a language model question-and-answer system based on a mixture of experts (MoE) architecture to analyze various manufacturing site data, such as manufacturing process, production facilities, and delivery schedule, in real time, and provide natural language-based answers corresponding to queries of workers.

sources.title: STAGED MIXED PARALLELISM REASONING METHOD AND SYSTEM FOR MOE SPARSE LARGE MODELS [US20260340345A1]
sources.abstract: The present disclosure provides a staged mixed parallelism reasoning method and system for an MoE sparse large model. The method includes: controlling the MoE sparse large model to execute the following steps layer by layer in a prefill stage: adding first MoE layer model parameters running based on a tensor parallelism strategy to each device while acquiring an expert number of each token of a prompt data sequence; then performing expert parallelism computation based on second MoE layer model parameters in each device running based on an expert parallelism strategy; restoring the tokens to device initial positions and releasing the second MoE layer model parameters; and sending a predicted token output by a last layer of the model to a first layer to execute reasoning in a decoding stage according to the predicted token and the first MoE layer model parameters in each device. The present disclosure can solve the problems that a parallelism strategy adopted by an existing MoE sparse large model reasoning technology has poor adaptability to the prefill stage and the decoding stage and large communication overhead.

sources.title: MIXTURE-OF-EXPERTS MODEL OPTIMIZATION METHOD, APPARATUS, AND DEVICE [WO2026223201A1]
sources.abstract: Embodiments of the present invention disclose a mixture-of-experts model optimization method, apparatus, and device. In the embodiments of the present invention, the method comprises: acquiring an average number of tokens of a mixture-of-experts model, the tokens being basic units used by the mixture-of-experts model to process input data; determining N times the average number of tokens of the mixture-of-experts model, N being an integer or a decimal greater than 1; and requesting allocation of target GPU memory on the basis of N times the average number of of tokens, the target GPU memory being configured to store tokens during a forward-propagation process. In the method, when allocation of GPU memory is requested during forward propagation, the GPU memory is allocated on the basis of N times the average number of tokens, thereby solving the problem of GPU memory fragmentation, reducing the GPU memory occupied by the mixture-of-experts model, and achieving optimization of the mixture-of-experts model.

sources.title: Method and System for Agent-Based Semantic Characterization and Self-Supervised Validation of Electronic Components Using Simulation and Expert Feedback [US20260330113A1]
sources.abstract: A system and method for semantic characterization and validation of electronic components using a Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) agent architecture. The system comprises: (1) a content orchestration agent responsible for extraction and normalization of device datasheet information, and (2) a simulation-generation agent which produces subcircuit models using a structured grammar and validates them via self-supervised SPICE simulations. The agents collaborate iteratively to construct scenarios reflective of real-world operating conditions, bridging the gap between idealized datasheet curves and actual component behavior. Simulation results are analyzed using clustering algorithms to form a performance taxonomy, enabling deterministic classification, similarity analysis, and circuit design recommendations.

NPU-Friendly Token Routing for Mixture-of-Experts Based Large Language Models on Edge Devices [US20260320352A1]
sources.abstract: [0000]    A neural processing unit (NPU) controls the routing of input tokens to experts in a mixture-of-experts (MoE) network. The NPU generates a routing table having a batch dimension of Bs and an expert dimension of N. Each element in the routing table is a probability value of routing an input token to an expert. The NPU further generates an expert selection vector indicating K top-ranked experts for each input token by performing quantization operations and rectified linear operations on N probability values along the expert dimension of the routing table with respect to the input token. The NPU further generates N sets of one-hot expert projection vectors for respective experts based on the routing table and expert selection vectors for the Bs input tokens. The N sets of one-hot expert project vectors are used to select the input tokens to dispatch to the experts.

sources.title: Aerial image classification system [US12762840B1]
sources.abstract: An aerial image classification system includes an unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV), a camera, a memory and a local processor. The UAV is wirelessly connected to a central server unit having a central processor that processes images obtained from the camera of the UAV to generate adaptively scaled spatial representations, applies a Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architecture to the adaptively scaled spatial representations, assigns weights to expert blocks of the MoE, processes adaptively scaled spatial representations based on the weights of the plurality of expert blocks, combines outputs of the expert blocks to generate an aggregated feature representation; and classifies the input image based on the aggregated feature representation.

sources.title: Robust adaptive beam forming method under small sample of array radar and communication system [CN122796348A]
authors: THE 54TH RESEARCH INST OF CHINA ELECTRONICS TECHNOLOGY GROUP CORPORATION
NANJING UNIV OF SCIENCE AND TECHNOLOGY
sources.organization: THE 54TH RESEARCH INST OF CHINA ELECTRONICS TECHNOLOGY GROUP CORPORATION, NANJING UNIV OF SCIENCE AND TECHNOLOGY
sources.abstract: The invention discloses a robust adaptive beam forming method under a small sample of an array radar and a communication system, and belongs to the field of array signal processing. Aiming at the problem that the performance of an array with amplitude-phase errors is obviously reduced under limited training samples, the method comprises the following steps: firstly, establishing a spatial domain sparse model of interference power, and reconstructing a covariance matrix of a received signal by estimating the amplitude-phase errors existing in an array channel and the power of an interference signal; thirdly, joint solving is carried out on the problems through an alternate optimization algorithm; and then, further obtaining an estimated value of a covariance matrix of the received signal by using the estimated amplitude-phase error and interference power. And finally, calculating a weight of adaptive beam forming under a minimum variance undistorted response criterion, and realizing robust adaptive beam forming. According to the method, the robustness of adaptive beam forming of the non-ideal linear array under small samples is effectively improved.

sources.title: Edge MoE reasoning-oriented heterogeneous storage and calculation integrated accelerator and reasoning method [CN122779297A]
sources.abstract: The invention discloses a heterogeneous storage and calculation integrated accelerator oriented to edge MoE reasoning and a reasoning method. The accelerator comprises a plurality of NPU cores and a two-dimensional grid network-on-chip, wherein each core comprises a storage and calculation integrated array, a network-on-chip interface and a scheduler. The array comprises a plurality of storage pages, each storage page is provided with a page lock register, a specified page is set to be in a locked state or an unlocked state in response to a page locking or page unlocking instruction, and the weight of the locked state is resident. And the hardware multicast unit sends data frames to a plurality of target cores in parallel to realize parallel transmission. And the scheduler distributes instructions to each functional unit in the NPU core. According to the invention, coexistence of weight residence and dynamic switching is realized on the same chip through a page lock mechanism. Under the conditions that the network contention is low and the receiving state of each target core is ready, the hardware multicast enables the path completion time of one-to-many transmission to be determined by the maximum path delay. And the scheduler queries expert positions through an expert position mapping table to realize reasoning acceleration of the edge MoE large language model.

sources.title: Model quantification method and device, electronic equipment, storage medium and program product [CN122779148A]
sources.abstract: Embodiments of the invention disclose a model quantification method and apparatus, an electronic device, a storage medium and a program product. The method comprises the steps of inputting a pre-constructed calibration set into a to-be-quantified hybrid expert MoE model for forward calculation; in the forward calculation process, responding to the fact that a current linear layer in the MoE model belongs to an expert layer, taking a score corresponding to an expert selected by a gating unit in the expert layer as a first weight factor, and obtaining a Hessian matrix based on the first weight factor; based on the Hessian matrix, the MoE model to be quantized is quantized, so that the influence of expert balance is added to Hessian matrix statistics, weighting is realized by selecting scores corresponding to experts in a gating unit on the Hessian matrix, and the generalization of model quantization is improved.

sources.title: End-to-end model architecture capable of being called by cockpit [CN122770759A]
authors: ANHUI JIANGHUAI AUTOMOBILE GROUP CORP LTD
sources.organization: ANHUI JIANGHUAI AUTOMOBILE GROUP CORP LTD
sources.abstract: The invention discloses an end-to-end model architecture capable of being called by a cockpit, and the architecture comprises an input module which receives a camera image, laser radar point cloud data, millimeter-wave radar point cloud data, vehicle positioning information and high-definition map data, converts the data into a corresponding data format, and inputs the data into a sensing layer; the perception layer performs feature fusion on the image and radar point cloud data to obtain 3D perception and 4D perception of obstacle information, lane line information and traffic light information, and outputs the 3D perception and 4D perception to the knowledge injection layer; the knowledge injection layer fuses a set rule, a sensing result and a common sense and then outputs the fused result to the decision-making layer; the decision-making layer carries out dynamic reasoning in an MoE mode, outputs decisions of car following, turning, obstacle avoidance, stopping, acceleration and deceleration, obtains a target track and transmits the target track to the output module; and the output module converts the target track into acceleration and wheel deflection angles and transmits the acceleration and the wheel deflection angles to corresponding control layers for intelligent driving control. The computing power demand of the intelligent driving model can be reduced, and the power consumption is reduced.

sources.title: Single-snapshot direction-of-arrival estimation method based on fractional order regularization decomposition gradient sparse reconstruction and mesh refinement [CN122776151A]
authors: THE 715TH RESEARCH INST OF CHINA STATE SHIPBUILDING CORPORATION LIMITED
sources.organization: THE 715TH RESEARCH INST OF CHINA STATE SHIPBUILDING CORPORATION LIMITED
sources.abstract: The invention relates to a single-snapshot direction of arrival estimation method based on fractional order regularization decomposition gradient sparse reconstruction and mesh refinement, and the method comprises the following steps: 1, constructing a far-field sparse model, and building a BPDN solving framework; step 2, coarse grid iteration: traversing a fractional order regularization parameter interval, and iteratively solving a BPDN optimization problem by adopting a decomposition gradient method to obtain a coarse grid spatial spectrum corresponding to each fractional order parameter; according to the method, the calculation cost is reduced, and meanwhile, the estimation precision and robustness under the single snapshot condition are remarkably improved.

sources.title: METHOD OF ADJUSTING MODEL AND RELATED DEVICE [WO2026192469A1]
sources.organization: HUAWEI TECH CO LTD, SMOLNIKOVA POLINA SERGEEVNA
sources.abstract: Embodiments of the present application provide a method of adjusting a model and related devices for adjusting a model. This method includes: obtaining a gating network logit value of each expert network in a first MoE layer corresponding to each token in T tokens based on the T tokens and a target MoE model; obtaining К selected expert networks corresponding to each token in the T tokens based on the logit value of each expert network in the first MoE layer corresponding to each token in the T tokens; obtaining an adjusted first MoE layer by pruning at least one expert network in the first MoE layer based on the К selected expert networks corresponding to each token in the T tokens; obtaining an adjusted target MoE model based on the adjusted first MoE layer. The proposed technique is applied for each MoE model layer in layer-by-layer manner and adjusts a MoE model to reduce a cost of resources required for deploying the MoE model.
